issues.legal_issue: A later suit is not barred by omission or relinquishment in an earlier suit when the two suits arise from distinct causes of action.
material_facts: Two legatees previously sued to protect properties from an alleged threatened alienation and stated that they reserved their rights concerning other properties for separate proceedings.

The later suit sought partition and other relief concerning different scheduled properties after the life-estate holder had died, when the legatees’ right to possession and enjoyment became enforceable.
The earlier protective suit was brought while the life-estate holder was alive, and the cause of action for the later suit depended on her subsequent death.
issues.conclusion: The later suit was not barred by Order II Rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure because it arose from a distinct cause of action.
issues.legal_principle: Order II Rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure require a plaintiff to include claims and available reliefs arising from a particular cause of action, and may bar a later suit for an omitted claim or relief arising from the same cause. The controlling requirement is identity of cause of action, not merely overlap in property or possible relief. The Court relied on Virgo Industries (Eng.) (P) Ltd. v. Venturetech Solutions (P) Ltd. and the explanation of cause of action in Mohammad Khalil Khan v. Mahbub Ali Mian.

rule.if: later_civil_suit and earlier_protective_suit and later_right_depended_on_later_event and distinct_causes_of_action

predicates.later_civil_suit: A party brought a later civil suit seeking a claim or relief concerning property.
predicates.earlier_protective_suit: The party had earlier brought a suit to protect an asserted interest against a threatened act concerning some property.
predicates.later_right_depended_on_later_event: The asserted right or ability to seek the later relief depended on an event occurring after the earlier suit was brought.
predicates.distinct_causes_of_action: The factual basis for the later relief was distinct from the factual basis for the earlier protective relief.
predicates.later_suit_not_barred: The later suit may proceed despite the earlier omission or relinquishment.

issues.definition: When a later civil suit rests on a distinct cause of action, including one dependent on a later event, it is not barred merely because an earlier protective suit omitted related relief.

issues.legal_issue: When both attesting witnesses to a will are unavailable, proof under the applicable alternative method does not require proof of both witnesses’ attestations, but does require proof of the testator’s signature and the handwriting of at least one attesting witness.
material_facts: Both attesting witnesses to the will had died by the relevant time.
A deposition by one attesting witness from earlier proceedings was produced; the witness described being asked to attest the will and identified his own signature on it.
The executor’s earlier testimony and a witness’s testimony in the present proceedings supported the testator’s signature on the will.
The earlier deposition was given in a proceeding in which the relevant interests were represented and the adverse party had an opportunity to cross-examine.
issues.conclusion: The earlier deposition was relevant under Section 33 of the Evidence Act, and the evidence satisfied Section 69’s requirements for proof of the will’s execution; Section 69 did not require proof of attestation by both witnesses.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 63 of the Indian Succession Act and 68 of the Evidence Act govern proof of an attested will when an attesting witness is available; Section 69 applies when no such witness can be found and requires proof that the testator’s signature and the attestation of at least one witness are in that person’s handwriting. Section 33 of the Evidence Act permits prior testimony when its conditions are met, including representation of interests and an opportunity to cross-examine. The Court relied on Babu Singh v. Ram Sahai and K. Laxmanan v. Thekkayil Padmini, and on the Privy Council’s interpretation of “representatives in interest” in Krishnayya Surya Rao Bahadur Garu v. Venkata Kumara Mahitathi Surya Rao Bahadur Garu.

rule.if: will_proof_proceeding and both_attesting_witnesses_unavailable and prior_testimony_conditions_met and testator_signature_proved and one_witness_handwriting_proved

predicates.will_proof_proceeding: A court is deciding whether a will has been proved.
predicates.both_attesting_witnesses_unavailable: Both witnesses who attested the will are unavailable to give evidence.
predicates.prior_testimony_conditions_met: A witness’s evidence from an earlier judicial proceeding is admissible because the required interests were represented, cross-examination was available, and the issues were substantially the same.
predicates.testator_signature_proved: Evidence establishes that the signature on the will is the testator’s handwriting.
predicates.one_witness_handwriting_proved: Evidence establishes that the attestation of at least one witness is in that witness’s handwriting.
predicates.will_execution_proved: The will’s execution is proved under the alternative method of proof.

issues.definition: If both attesting witnesses are unavailable and the testator’s signature and one witness’s attestation are proved using admissible evidence, execution of the will is proved without proving both attestations.

issues.legal_issue: Secondary evidence of a registered will may be admitted when the original was produced in earlier proceedings and is no longer available from the person who had it.
material_facts: The trial court found that the original will had been produced in earlier proceedings.
The executor, who had retained the original, had died.
The executor’s son was asked to produce the original and stated that he did not possess it.
A certified copy of the registered will was tendered as secondary evidence.
issues.conclusion: The admission of the certified copy as secondary evidence was justified, and the contrary view of the High Court could not stand.
issues.legal_principle: The Court upheld the concurrent factual finding that the circumstances warranted admitting secondary evidence of the will. It distinguished the question of whether the will was proved from objections to the use of a certified copy, and relied on the evidence concerning the original’s earlier production and subsequent unavailability.

rule.if: will_proof_proceeding and original_previously_produced and custodian_unavailable and current_holder_lacks_original and certified_copy_available

predicates.will_proof_proceeding: A court is deciding whether a will has been proved.
predicates.original_previously_produced: The original document was produced in an earlier proceeding.
predicates.custodian_unavailable: The person who had custody of the original is no longer available to produce it.
predicates.current_holder_lacks_original: A person asked to produce the original states that they do not possess it.
predicates.certified_copy_available: A certified copy of the document is available for use as secondary evidence.
predicates.secondary_evidence_admissible: The certified copy may be admitted as secondary evidence in the circumstances.

issues.definition: A certified copy may be admitted when the original was earlier produced, its custodian is unavailable, and a person asked to produce it does not possess it.

issues.legal_issue: A coparcener’s declaration to separate does not effect severance unless it is communicated to the other affected coparcener before the declarant’s death, and a will cannot dispose of an undivided coparcenary interest under the pre-existing law.
material_facts: The parties’ claimed oral partition was not proved.
A newspaper notice purporting to declare separation was dated after the date on which the alleged response from the other coparcener was said to have been sent.
The alleged correspondence showing communication was not produced in the civil proceedings, and the evidence about its dates and contents was inconsistent.
There was no other evidence that the other coparcener knew of the declaration before the declarant died.
The declarant died before the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 came into force.
issues.conclusion: The court could not find that severance had been effected before the declarant’s death; consequently, the will could not dispose of the disputed properties as the declarant’s separate property.
issues.legal_principle: A severance of joint-family status requires an unequivocal intention to separate communicated to the affected coparcener; knowledge must be established, and a later communication cannot defeat rights that vested on the death. A will speaks from the testator’s death, and under the law applicable before Section 30 of the Hindu Succession Act, a coparcener could not bequeath an undivided interest in joint-family property. The Court relied on Addagada Raghavamma v. Addagada Chenchamma, Girja Bai v. Sadashiv Dhundiraj, and the principles concerning the effect of severance and joint-family property in Bhagwant P. Sulakhe v. Digambar Gopal Sulakhe.

rule.if: coparcenary_title_proceeding and no_proved_prior_partition and separation_declaration_not_proved_communicated_before_death and death_before_testamentary_change

predicates.coparcenary_title_proceeding: The proceeding concerns title to property claimed to belong to a Hindu coparcenary.
predicates.no_proved_prior_partition: The asserted earlier partition among the coparceners is not proved.
predicates.separation_declaration_not_proved_commun: The evidence does not establish that the other affected coparcener knew of an unequivocal declaration to separate before the declarant died.
predicates.death_before_testamentary_change: The coparcener died before a change in law permitted testamentary disposition of an undivided coparcenary interest.
predicates.severance_not_established_and_will_canno: The declaration does not establish severance before death, and the will cannot dispose of the undivided interest as separate property.

issues.definition: If a prior partition is unproved and communication of a declaration to separate before death is also unproved, there is no established severance and the will cannot dispose of the undivided interest under the earlier law.

issues.legal_issue: A female Hindu’s limited interest is enlarged into absolute ownership when it rests on a pre-existing right, including a right to maintenance, rather than a new restricted interest created by an instrument.
material_facts: The widow had a pre-existing right to maintenance and, upon her husband’s death while the property remained joint, acquired an interest under the Hindu Women’s Right to Property Act, 1937.
She asserted rights to the property and sought partition and possession in the earlier suit.
The will, if treated as operative, provided the widow with a life interest and directed that income from the properties be used for her expenses and for specified family purposes.
The widow later entered into a compromise under which she gave up her rights in the properties at issue in favour of the other branch.
issues.conclusion: Section 14(1), rather than Section 14(2), applied; the widow’s limited interest became absolute, and the compromise by which she gave up her rights supported the other branch’s title.
issues.legal_principle: Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 enlarges a female Hindu’s limited interest where the property is possessed under a pre-existing right, including maintenance; Section 14(2) applies to a new and independent restricted grant, not an instrument recognising such a right. Section 3(2) of the Hindu Women’s Right to Property Act, 1937 gave a widow an interest in joint-family property, and the Court considered the meaning of possession under Section 14(1). It relied on V. Tulasamma v. Sesha Reddy, Mst. Karmi v. Amru, Gummalapura Taggina Matada Kotturuswami v. Setra Veeravva, Mangal Singh v. Smt. Rattno, Eramma v. Veerupana, and distinguished Sadhu Singh v. Gurdwara Sahib Narike.

rule.if: female_property_right_proceeding and pre_existing_maintenance_or_statutory_right and property_possessed_under_claim_of_right and interest_recognises_existing_right

predicates.female_property_right_proceeding: A court is determining the extent of a female Hindu’s interest in property.
predicates.pre_existing_maintenance_or_statutory_ri: The female Hindu had an existing right to maintenance or another legally recognised right in the property before the instrument or event said to limit her interest.
predicates.property_possessed_under_claim_of_right: She possessed or claimed the property under a legally recognisable right, rather than as a mere trespasser.
predicates.interest_recognises_existing_right: The limited interest recognises or provides for an existing right instead of creating an independent new interest subject to restriction.
predicates.limited_interest_enlarged_to_absolute_ow: The female Hindu’s limited interest becomes absolute ownership.

issues.definition: A female Hindu’s limited interest becomes absolute when she possesses or claims the property under a pre-existing right and the interest recognises that right.

issues.legal_issue: Earlier compromises and related proceedings do not bar a later claim to property when the claimants were not bound by the compromise and the later cause of action is distinct.
material_facts: The widow’s earlier suit ended in a compromise in which she gave up rights in some properties and received rights in others.
The claimants under the will were not parties to that compromise.
A later suit by some claimants concerned only a subset of the properties and expressly reserved claims to other properties.
A subsequent partition suit was brought by parties who were not parties to that later suit.
The compromise proceedings did not adjudicate the disputed title on its merits.
issues.conclusion: The earlier compromises and the claimants’ conduct did not establish estoppel, waiver, acquiescence, or abandonment of their claims to the properties in the later suit; respondents who were not parties to the subsequent suit could not rely on estoppel based on it.
issues.legal_principle: A compromise and a party’s conduct do not, without more, extinguish a property right that is otherwise established; the effect of proceedings depends on the parties, the properties at issue, and the right asserted. The Court relied on Sha Mulchand & Co. Ltd. v. Jawahar Mills Limited and Dr. Karan Singh v. State of J&K, as well as its analysis of the distinct causes of action in the earlier and later suits.

rule.if: later_property_claim and claimants_not_bound_by_earlier_compromise and earlier_suit_limited_or_right_reserved and alleged_estoppel_based_on_proceeding_without_same_parties

predicates.later_property_claim: A party brings a later claim asserting an interest in property.
predicates.claimants_not_bound_by_earlier_compromis: The later claimants were not parties to, and were not bound by, the earlier compromise.
predicates.earlier_suit_limited_or_right_reserved: The earlier suit concerned only some properties or expressly reserved claims to other property.
predicates.alleged_estoppel_based_on_proceeding_wit: A party seeks to prevent the later claim by relying on conduct or a proceeding to which the relevant opposing parties were not all parties.
predicates.earlier_conduct_does_not_bar_later_claim: The earlier compromise or conduct does not bar the later property claim.

issues.definition: A later property claim is not barred by an earlier compromise or proceeding when the claimants were not bound by it and the earlier proceeding was limited or reserved other claims.

issues.legal_issue: A purchaser cannot obtain title from a transferor who has no right in the property to convey.
material_facts: Purchasers claimed under sale deeds executed by a legatee who asserted title under the will.
The will did not confer an enforceable right to the disputed properties because severance before the testator’s death was not established.
The widow’s interest had become absolute and she had given up her rights in the disputed properties under the compromise.
The transferor therefore had no right in those properties to pass to the purchasers.
issues.conclusion: The purchasers acquired no enforceable title through the transferor, and their appeals were dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: A transferor cannot convey a greater title than the transferor possesses. Because the asserted testamentary title failed and the widow’s rights had become absolute before she relinquished them under the compromise, the transferor had no title to convey.

predicates.purchaser_claims_through_transferor: A purchaser bases title to property on a conveyance from another person.
predicates.transferor_has_no_title_to_property: The person who made the conveyance had no enforceable right in the property to transfer.
predicates.purchaser_acquires_no_title: The purchaser acquires no enforceable title through that conveyance.

issues.definition: A purchaser acquires no title when the purchaser relies on a conveyance from a person who had no enforceable title to transfer.
